entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Jallianwala Bagh massacre was a pivotal event in the struggle for Indian independence from British rule. On April 13, 1919, British Indian Army troops, led by General Reginald Dyer, fired into a crowd of unarmed Indian civilians in Amritsar's Jallianwala Bagh, killing over 1,000 people. This event shocked the nation and played a significant role in galvanizing the Indian independence movement. The massacre took place in the context of growing tensions between the British colonial authorities and the Indian people, who were demanding greater autonomy and self-governance. The event marked a turning point in the struggle for Indian independence, with many Indians viewing the British as brutal and oppressive. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre remains one of the most infamous incidents of colonial violence in Indian history and serves as a powerful symbol of the Indian people's long-standing struggle for freedom.

The massacre itself was sparked by a series of protests and demonstrations against the British colonial authorities, who had imposed strict regulations on the Indian population. The protests, which began in the spring of 1919, were met with brutal force by the British authorities, who saw the Indian people as a threat to their power and authority. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre was the culmination of these tensions, as British troops fired into the crowd of unarmed civilians, killing hundreds and injuring thousands more. The event was widely condemned by the Indian people and by many British citizens, who saw it as a clear example of the brutality and oppression of the British colonial authorities. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre played a significant role in shaping the Indian independence movement and paved the way for the eventual granting of independence to India in 1947.
